query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical behavior of solidified, Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by partial dislocation activity and stacking-fault-assisted twinning at high strain rates (≥10³ s⁻¹) and low-to-moderate temperatures (≤800 K), where twinning-triggered strain hardening enables the alloy’s strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified FeNiCrMn samples with controlled grain sizes, homogeneous chemistry, and minimal pre-existing defects.
generation.intervention: Systematic tensile and compressive tests at strain rates from 10⁻³ to 10⁴ s⁻¹ across temperatures ranging from cryogenic (~77 K) to 800 K.
generation.conditions: Maintain identical compositional and processing histories, varying only strain rate and temperature. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (TEM, EBSD) after deformation to assess dislocation density, stacking-fault formation, and twin evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial dislocation dissociation leading to stacking faults and {111} twin boundaries that impede dislocation glide.
generation.mechanism: As temperature decreases and strain rate increases, reduced stacking-fault energy enhances partial dislocation splitting, promoting stacking faults which nucleate mechanical twins. These twins increase strain hardening by providing additional barrier interfaces to dislocation movement, thus sustaining the strength–ductility balance under dynamic loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Higher strain rates and lower temperatures will correlate with an increase in mechanical twinning and fault density, resulting in elevated flow stress and improved strain hardening relative to quasi-static or high-temperature tests.
generation.baseline: At quasi-static loading and room temperature, limited twinning activity and moderate strain hardening have been observed in related high-/medium-entropy alloys; the proposed mechanism predicts a measurable increase in twinning and elevated work-hardening response under more extreme loading conditions.
generation.boundary: Applies to Co-free FeNiCrMn with fcc-based microstructure and moderate stacking-fault energy. May not extend to alternative compositions or systems with different phases or significantly altered stacking-fault energies.
generation.uncertainty: Exact contributions of localized shear banding, precipitates, or grain-boundary effects under rapid loading are less clear, and require controlled microstructural isolation. Temperature ranges above 800 K or ultrahigh rates (>10⁴ s⁻¹) remain insufficiently explored.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a matrix of split-Hopkinson bar and servo-hydraulic tests on FeNiCrMn samples with identical microstructures to measure stress–strain behavior at strain rates of 10⁻³ to 10⁴ s⁻¹ and temperatures from cryogenic to 800 K. Analyze post-deformation microstructures by TEM/EBSD to quantify twin boundary density and dislocation substructure.
measurements: Stress–strain curves and strain-hardening rates at each strain rate and temperature
Twin boundary and stacking-fault density from TEM/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If tests reveal a negligible increase in mechanical twinning or stacking faults at high strain rates or low temperatures, and the alloy fails to exhibit enhanced strain-hardening, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Currently, several EHEA systems have been developed, including AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [], Al17Ni34Ti17V32 [], AlCr1.3TiNi2 [], and AlCrCuFeNi2 []. Owing to better practicality and low cost, the AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy, with similar microstructure and properties to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, was investigated. It is indicated that the AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy consists of the FCC and A2/B2 spinodal decomposition phase and presents better fracture strength and ductility []. In addition, the dynamic mechanical response of HEAs has also received a lot of attention. To use HEAs in extreme industrial environments, there is an urgent need for a comprehensive understanding of their performance and mechanisms during high-speed compression [,,,,]. According to the available literature, in addition to the dislocation-related mechanism, twinning mechanism, grain boundary-related mechanism, diffusion creep mechanism, and dynamic recrystallization mechanism, the shear bands are formed in HEAs at high strain rates or under large deformation conditions [,,,,]. Figure 3(b) indicates that the high density of dislocations tends to align in one direction and entangle under dynamic loading. Such a high dislocation density configuration has been also observed for the laser-induced shock compression of monocrystalline copper. Mechanical twins form in many metallic materials, especially those with low stacking-fault energy (SFE). Some fcc single phase materials with high SFE (such as Al and Ni) may not easily form twins except under extreme conditions, such as low temperatures and high strain rates. Figure 3(c) shows that the parallel bands are mechanical twins, which suggests that mechanical twinning is an important plastic deformation mechanism in the Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy at high strain rates. Figure 3(d) summarizes the deformation mechanism of the Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA under dynamic loading, indicating that the dislocation slip and twinning can lead to the excellent strain-hardening ability.

The deformation mechanism in several HEAs has been reported to transition from dislocation-mediated to twinning-induced plasticity with increase in strain rate. Twin boundaries act as barriers for dislocation movement and increase the strain hardenability. The ability for twinning depends on the stacking fault energy (SFE), which for several FCC-based HEAs has been reported to be in the range of 20 to 30 mJ/m2. In low-SFE HEAs, dislocations dissociate into partials with large separation and require more thermal activation for cross-slip resulting in an increase in strain rate sensitivity (SRS). However, there is limited understanding of the microstructure evolution at high strain rates in the range of 103 s−1–105 s−1. Application of HEAs in high-speed loading conditions requires in-depth knowledge of their dynamic deformation behavior, such as in ballistic impact and penetration.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC6478865, 2019) on Al0.7CoCrFeNi under quasi-static and dynamic loading showed that precipitation and interface structures influence strain-rate sensitivity but did not isolate the mechanism for FeNiCrMn. Concurrently, nanoindentation tests (PMC6488616, 2019) on various Fe–Mn–Co–Cr-based HEAs revealed differing strain-rate sensitivities tied to phase stability and defect processes but provided limited insight into the Co-free FeNiCrMn regime. Later, molecular dynamics simulations (PMC8398136, 2021) in CoNiCrFeMn nanowires demonstrated temperature-dependent superplasticity governed by partial dislocations and phase transformations, again highlighting rate- and temperature-sensitivity without clarifying the Co-free composition’s controlling mechanism. Most recently, high-strain-rate compression of AlCrFe2Ni2 (PMC11943535, 2025) confirmed the role of dynamic shear localization and microstructural transformations in a Co-free system, but it did not address how stacking fault energy and twinning interact specifically in FeNiCrMn. Across these studies, despite different alloy chemistries and defect populations, it is clear that dynamic behavior depends strongly on loading conditions and microstructure, leaving the fundamental mechanism in Co-free FeNiCrMn still unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how partial dislocation activity, stacking fault energetics, and possible twinning combine to govern the dynamic strength–ductility response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn across varied temperatures and strain rates. Prior work on related alloys suggests that dislocation interactions and fault formation are crucial, but the core drivers of rate and temperature sensitivity in this specific composition have not been established.
decision.lever: Systematic high-strain-rate (10^−3 to 10^4 s^−1) and temperature (cryogenic to 800 K) tensile/compressive tests on FeNiCrMn samples with controlled grain sizes. Post-deformation microstructure analysis (e.g., using TEM/EBSD) would quantify partial dislocation, twin, and fault evolution across these conditions.
decision.why: A direct experimental approach, spanning relevant strain rates and temperatures while controlling the initial microstructure, will isolate whether partial dislocation- and twin-mediated plasticity dictates dynamic response. Observing enhanced twinning and faulting at lower temperatures and higher strain rates would support this mechanism. A contradictory result—such as a slip-dominated response with minimal twinning—would falsify this hypothesis.
